newsitem.title: USA: Jewish leaders scrap boycott plans of Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leaders scrap boycott plans of Swiss banks.

text.p: Jewish leaders on Thursday dropped plans to debate calling for a world-wide boycott of Swiss banks after the banks established a Holocaust memorial fund, a World Jewish Congress offical said.
"We have gone from confrontation to cooperation," WJC Vice president Kalman Sultanik said.
The boycott call was to have been discussed at a Feb. 14 meeting of the World Jewish Restitution Organisation, the WJC's reparations arms.
It was the most forceful of several options under consideration, including seeking to have Swiss bank licenses in New York state revoked.
But instead the meeting will be attended by Swiss and U.S. government representatives and will be used to discuss cooperative moves with Switzerland, Sultanik said.

Also expected to attend the meeting, which will be held in New York, is Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, the New York Republican who has emerged as Switzerland's sharpest critic in the United States.

Switzerland's three biggest banks, Union Bank of Switzerland, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp, announced on Wednesday that they would set up a $70 million memorial fund to aid Holocaust victims and invited the Swiss government and central bank to join the fund.
D'Amato called the fund "a start" but added that the money was "nowhere near enough."

The move by the banks capped months of pressure from Jewish groups, joined by the Clinton administration and D'Amato, on Swiss banks who were accused of hoarding millions of dollars deposited by Jews before and during the Second World War.
Decisions still have to be made on how the fund would be administered and who the beneficiaries would be but the fact that the fund has been established appears to have dramatically cooled tempers.

Swiss-Jewish relations reached a crisis point in early January after the outgoing Swiss President accused Jewish groups of blackmail and extortion by demanding that a memorial fund be set up even though Switzerland had just begun its own investigation.

Matters were not helped when it was discovered last month that Union Bank had shredded tonnes of documents from the 1930s and 40s that might have shed light on how Swiss banks handled Jewish accounts.
WJC members called for a boycott to be considered and the organisation responded by putting it on the agenda for the Feb. 14 meeting.
Even news that a boycott was being considered frayed nerves and rattled stock markets in Switzerland where banking is a major industry.

The New York State Assembly and New York City's Council got into the dispute with the assembly calling a hearing for next Wednesday to determine how it could revoke the license of a foreign bank operating in the state.
The City Council set a hearing for Monday on whether the nation's largest city should refuse to make deposits in Swiss banks unless a compensation fund was established.
The WJC on Wednesday informed the City Council that the Swiss had set up a memorial fund which met the council's conditions.
